title: Methods for Detection of Artefacts in EEG with Hemodynamic Recordings
author: Nuttall, El Mir, et al.

steps.title: Compute expected artefact parameters
steps.instruction: Enter the following acquisition parameters: repetition time (TR), total number of volumes, number of slices, number of dummy scans, and the sequence type. For volume‑based gradient‑switch (GS) detection set the expected number of artefacts equal to the number of volumes and the artefact duration equal to TR. For slice‑based detection set the expected number of artefacts equal to (volumes × slices) and the artefact duration equal to TR divided by the number of slices (no inter‑volume break). For multiband sequences use the number of RF pulses as the “number of slices”.

steps.title: Detect gradient switch artefacts
steps.instruction: Calculate the median of the maximum amplitude across all EEG channels and use this value as the initial peak‑detection threshold. Iterate through each channel, labeling all peaks above the threshold. Compute the interval between successive peaks; accept a channel only if the mode of these intervals is within two sampling points of the expected artefact duration and the total number of peaks is within ±7 of the expected artefact count (accounting for dummy scans). Display the labelled channel to the user for confirmation; if unsatisfactory, repeat on the next channel until an acceptable one is found. Once a channel is chosen, delete the first N peaks where N equals the number of dummy scans. The remaining peak times constitute the GS artefact onset vector, ready for input to correction algorithms.

steps.title: High‑pass filter and segment EEG
steps.instruction: Apply a FIR high‑pass filter with cutoff >1 Hz, transition bandwidth = 1 Hz, and filter order = 5 to the continuous EEG data. Segment the filtered data into non‑overlapping blocks of a user‑specified length (e.g., 20 s for the present analysis).

steps.title: Select reference cardiac artefact per segment
steps.instruction: For each segment, display the data (starting with the first channel) and allow the user to scroll through channels to find the one that best shows the cardiac‑ballistocardiogram (CB) artefact. The user manually selects the peaks of two consecutive, clear CB artefacts. Compute the inter‑peak distance RtoR. Extract the data surrounding each selected peak from (peak − RtoR/2) to (peak + RtoR/2). Zero‑mean each extracted waveform and average the two to obtain the reference artefact for that segment.

steps.title: Derive mean artefact from segment peaks
steps.instruction: Detect all additional peaks in the same segment using a minimum peak distance of (RtoR − 10) sampling points. For each detected peak, calculate the Pearson correlation with the reference artefact; retain only peaks with r ≥ 0.7. Average the retained peaks to create the mean artefact (convolution kernel) for the segment.

steps.title: Detect cardiac artefact onsets via convolution
steps.instruction: Convolve the chosen channel’s segment data with the mean artefact obtained above. In the convolved signal, automatically locate peaks that satisfy: (i) peak prominence ≥ 2 standard deviations above the convolved‑signal mean, and (ii) inter‑peak distance ≥ 0.8 × (length of the mean artefact). Record the times of these peaks as the CB artefact onsets for the segment.

steps.title: Combine artefact onset vectors
steps.instruction: Repeat steps 4–6 for every segment, concatenating the CB artefact onset times from each segment into a single vector. The final vectors of GS and CB artefact onsets can then be supplied to standard artefact‑correction pipelines.
